identity.title: Aligner: Efficient Alignment by Learning to Correct

problem.claim: Develop an efficient alignment method for evolving LLM deployment requirements and rapid iteration.

gap.claim: Existing alignment methods are portrayed as too complex for rapid deployment iteration, motivating a model-agnostic approach.

contributions.claim: Introduces Aligner, a small-model paradigm that learns correctional residuals between preferred and dispreferred answers.
Presents Aligner as a one-off-trained, model-agnostic plug-and-play module for open-source and API-based upstream models.
Describes iterative bootstrapping of upstream models with corrected responses used as synthetic preference data.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors characterize Aligner as a novel and simple alignment paradigm that separates correction learning into a small, reusable module.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report improvements when deploying the same Aligner model across 11 LLMs evaluated on helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty.
The authors report that Aligner-7B produced average gains of 68.9% in helpfulness and 22.8% in harmlessness across tested LLMs, while reducing hallucination.
A community-reported Alpaca-Eval result states that stacking Aligner-2B on GPT-4 Turbo raised LC Win Rate from 55.0% to 58.3%, above GPT-4 Omni's 57.5%.

narrative_sequence.summary: Rapidly changing LLM requirements create pressure for efficient alignment and fast deployment iteration.
Aligner learns answer-correction residuals with a small model and is intended to plug into varied upstream models after one-off training.
The proposed module can iteratively bootstrap upstream models using corrected responses as synthetic preference data.
The authors report cross-model 3H improvements, including average gains for Aligner-7B; separately, a community report describes a leaderboard gain from stacking Aligner-2B on GPT-4 Turbo.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a modular design claim with a cross-model test using the same Aligner model across 11 LLMs.

lessons.interpretation: Testing reuse across heterogeneous targets directly supports the proposed model-agnostic deployment story.
lessons.application: When claiming portability, evaluate one fixed module across multiple target models and report the shared training/setup conditions.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the method is intentionally specialized to one architecture or domain.

source_observation.claim: The abstract reports both aggregate dimension-specific gains and a concrete leaderboard comparison with named baselines and win rates.

lessons.interpretation: Pairing broad summary metrics with an externally recognizable comparison makes the claimed impact easier to contextualize.
lessons.application: Report aggregate task or dimension changes together with a concrete benchmark comparison, preserving metric definitions and provenance.
lessons.exception: Avoid leaderboard comparisons when scores use incompatible protocols or the comparison source is not clearly identified.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, evaluation protocols, sample sizes, statistical uncertainty, or baseline details for the 11-model experiments.
The hallucination-reduction claim has no quantified result in the supplied units.
The Alpaca-Eval comparison is explicitly identified as a community report; its evaluation conditions are not given.
The abstract does not report evidence for the iterative bootstrapping or performance-ceiling claim.

editorial_revisions.before: Experiments report cross-model 3H improvements, including substantial average gains for Aligner-7B and a leaderboard gain from stacking Aligner-2B on GPT-4 Turbo.
editorial_revisions.after: The authors report cross-model 3H improvements, including average gains for Aligner-7B; separately, a community report describes a leaderboard gain from stacking Aligner-2B on GPT-4 Turbo.
